doc.title: Wilson "Chembo" Corniel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

title: Growing up in New York with Latin roots and salsa as foundation
summary: Corniel grew up amid rock and Motown but absorbed Tito Rodriguez and Machito at home and began in salsa bands; he explains the roles of each percussion instrument.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: It is part of it, but the thing is when I was born and raised in New York City so I had all these other influences around me, you know, like I grew up with the Beatles, Motown, Glen Campbell, Willie Nelson, the Temptations, Rolling Stones. You know so it’s a whole mixture of different things besides my Latin roots that I picked up at home, the records that my mother played, the Tito Rodriguez, Machito, all the ballad singers, you know, so that’s always been in my ear, the Latin part, besides my surroundings growing up you know, as a whole, as a musician as a whole. But as I grew up and played my conga drums I played with — I started off playing with salsa bands, salsa, you know, Latin music. And that’s my foundation, salsa music. So by listening to records and listening and knowing what the combination is with the percussion — you know we have to be percussionists. We have a timbale player, you know, bongo player, for a traditional salsa set up. So you have to know the functions of each drum to work as unison, as one. It’s not just banging away. There’s a chemistry, there’s a technique in order for it to mesh. And that technique, you’ve got to learn, you’ve got to know the basic patterns of that in order for you to grow and for you to do any other Latin style, that is the key to hold up. If you want to do a Latin tune for your club date band, if you know those components, and then you can start up and do a little basic that’s not going to be watered down but it’s going to be authentic.
